settings.title: The Years Between Closing and Dissolving

settings.editor:
A restaurant closing is rarely tidy. The lease ends or gets assigned, the equipment goes to an auctioneer or stays in a unit nobody has emptied, the staff are paid out, and the corporation that held it all is quietly left alone. Owners move on to the next thing and the entity stays on the registry, accumulating filing years nobody is watching.

Those years matter, because the corporation cannot be dissolved while any of them is unfiled. The year the restaurant actually closed is almost never nil, since equipment is sold and accounts are settled. The years after it, once everything has gone, usually are, and each of those is $300.00 plus HST per tax year.

settings.title: When a Closed Restaurant Corporation Is Not Nil

settings.description_text: An auction, a private sale or a transfer of the kitchen to the next tenant is a disposal with a gain or loss to report.
A returned deposit, an assignment payment or a negotiated exit from the landlord is money moving through the corporation.
Outstanding gift cards honoured elsewhere, or written off, change the liability on the books.
A refunded liquor, food premises or municipal licence fee is income in the year it is received.

settings.editor:
The closing year is the complicated one and it is worth getting right. Equipment sold for less than its depreciated value produces a terminal loss, which is a deduction, and a corporation that simply stops filing never claims it. Staff final pay, the GST/HST on an asset sale and the lease settlement all land in that same year.

settings.title_text: A Terminal Loss Is Worth Claiming
settings.description_text: Kitchen equipment usually sells below its depreciated value. That difference is a deduction in the closing year.
A loan owed to or from an owner stays on the balance sheet until it is repaid or written off.
Both accounts stay open until they are closed on their own forms. The T2 does not touch either.

settings.html:
The year is nil

  • No sales were made and no service was run in the tax year
  • No equipment, fixtures or leaseholds were sold or transferred
  • No lease deposit, licence refund or rebate was received
  • No supplier, staff or rent cost was claimed by the corporation
  • No shareholder loan was repaid or written off in the year

The year is not nil

  • Kitchen equipment or fixtures were auctioned, sold or handed over
  • The lease was assigned, surrendered or settled with the landlord
  • A liquor, food premises or municipal licence fee was refunded
  • Outstanding gift cards were redeemed or written off
  • Any staff payment or final payroll ran in the year

Due either way

  • A T2 for every year until the corporation is dissolved
  • A T183CORP signed by an authorised signing officer, per tax year
  • The GST/HST account, closed on Form RC145 rather than abandoned
  • The payroll account, which expects filings until it is closed
  • The clearance certificate, which no unfiled year will allow

Closed restaurant corporations are filed the same way wherever the registered office sits, because the return is prepared and transmitted electronically from end to end. There is nothing to print, nothing to post and nothing to sign in person.

Where the corporation was incorporated changes the registry, not the return. An Ontario corporation answers to the Ontario Business Registry, and corporations in British Columbia, Alberta, Quebec and Saskatchewan each answer to their own. The T2 itself is federal and identical in all of them. Within Ontario, a corporation registered in Toronto, Mississauga, Brampton or Ottawa is filed on the same terms and at the same price as one anywhere else in the country.

Two provinces add a return the federal T2 does not cover. A Quebec corporation also files the CO-17 and an Alberta corporation also files the AT1. Both are separate provincial returns, and neither is included in the $300.00 plus HST fee.

settings.editor: A T2 for each of those three years and for every year since, until the corporation is dissolved. The closing year itself is usually an ordinary return rather than a nil one.
No. A disposal produces a gain or, far more often with restaurant equipment, a terminal loss. That is a deduction worth claiming, and it makes the year an ordinary T2.
No. A clearance certificate will not be issued while a year is outstanding, and dissolution adds a final T2 due within six months of the dissolution date.
It stays open and expects returns until it is closed on Form RC145. Closing the restaurant does not close the account, and the T2 does not either.
Yes, separately. A payroll account expects filings until it is closed, even where no wages were paid after the closure.
It can be, as long as nothing was repaid or written off during the year. The balance is reported on Schedule 100, and a balance sitting still is not activity.
The year it was received. A returned deposit is money moving through the corporation, so that year is not nil.
The outstanding balance is a liability. Writing it off or honouring it changes the books and takes that year out of nil.
One authorised signing officer signs the T183CORP for each tax year. Every shareholder at 10% or more is still listed on Schedule 50.
File the outstanding years. A demand is usually followed by an arbitrary assessment on figures the Agency invents, and the real returns are what replace them.
